cfr-1024.210-release_holdout-00.text:
31 CFR § 1024.210

This provision requires mutual funds to develop and implement a written anti-money laundering (AML) program approved by their board of directors or trustees. The program must, at a minimum, include: (1) internal policies, procedures, and controls; (2) a designated compliance officer; (3) ongoing employee training; and (4) an independent audit function to test the program.

cfr-1024.210-release_holdout-01.text:
31 CFR § 1024.210

This provision requires mutual funds to develop and implement a written anti-money laundering (AML) program approved by their board of directors or trustees, including minimum program elements such as internal controls, independent testing, designated compliance personnel, and ongoing training.

cfr-1024.210-release_holdout-02.text:
31 CFR § 1024.210

This section requires mutual funds to develop and implement a written anti-money laundering (AML) program, approved by their board of directors or trustees, that is designed to prevent the fund from being used for money laundering or terrorist financing. The program must, at a minimum, include: (1) internal policies, procedures, and controls; (2) designation of a compliance officer; (3) ongoing employee training; and (4) independent testing for compliance.

cfr-1024.210-release_holdout-04.text: The governing provision requires mutual funds to implement and approve a written anti-money laundering (AML) program, which must be approved by the fund’s board of directors or trustees and include, at a minimum: (1) the development of internal policies, procedures, and controls; (2) designation of a compliance officer; (3) ongoing employee training; and (4) an independent audit function to test the program. Citation: 31 CFR § 1024.210.

cfr-1024.410-release_holdout-00.text:
31 CFR § 1010.420

This provision requires mutual funds to retain records of the information used to verify the identity of customers, and it points to the general recordkeeping requirements found in 31 CFR § 1010.410.

cfr-1024.410-release_holdout-01.text:
31 CFR § 1010.420

This provision requires mutual funds to retain records of the issuance of shares, referencing the general recordkeeping requirements applicable to financial institutions.

cfr-1024.410-release_holdout-02.text:
31 CFR § 1024.400

This provision requires mutual funds to comply with the general recordkeeping requirements found in 31 CFR § 1010.410, thereby incorporating those broader obligations by reference specifically for mutual funds.

cfr-1024.410-release_holdout-03.text: The mutual-fund-specific recordkeeping provision requires mutual funds to comply with the general recordkeeping requirements applicable to banks, including limits such as retaining records of certain transactions for five years. cfr-1024.410-release_holdout-04.text: The governing provision states that mutual funds must comply with the general recordkeeping requirements applicable to banks under the Bank Secrecy Act. Citation: 31 CFR § 1024.400.

cfr-1026.210-release_holdout-00.text:
31 CFR § 1026.210

This provision requires futures commission merchants and introducing brokers in commodities to implement and maintain a written anti-money laundering (AML) program, approved in writing by senior management. The program must, at a minimum, include: (1) policies, procedures, and internal controls; (2) designation of a compliance officer; (3) ongoing employee training; and (4) independent testing for compliance.

cfr-1026.210-release_holdout-01.text:
31 CFR § 1026.210

cfr-1026.210-release_holdout-02.text:
31 CFR § 1026.210

cfr-1026.210-release_holdout-04.text: The governing provision requires that each futures commission merchant and introducing broker develop and implement an anti-money laundering program approved in writing by senior management, and specifies minimum elements such as internal policies, designation of a compliance officer, ongoing training, and independent testing. Citation: 31 CFR § 1026.210.

cfr-1026.320-release_holdout-00.text:
31 CFR § 1026.320

Futures commission merchants and introducing brokers must file a suspicious activity report no later than 30 calendar days after the initial detection of facts that may constitute a basis for filing, or within 60 days if no suspect is identified.

cfr-1026.320-release_holdout-01.text:
31 CFR § 1026.320

This provision requires futures commission merchants and introducing brokers in commodities to file a suspicious activity report no later than 30 calendar days after the initial detection of facts that may constitute a basis for filing such a report.

31 CFR § 1026.320

31 CFR § 1026.410

cfr-1026.410-release_holdout-01.text:
31 CFR § 1026.410

This provision requires futures commission merchants and introducing brokers in commodities to comply with the general recordkeeping requirements set forth in 31 CFR § 1010.410.

cfr-1026.410-release_holdout-02.text:
31 CFR § 1026.410

cfr-1027.100-release_holdout-00.text:
31 CFR § 1027.100

The covered-goods definition for dealers in jewels, precious metals, and precious stones—including finished goods—is governed by this section, which defines "covered goods" as jewels, precious metals, or precious stones, whether in raw or finished form, that are bought or sold in the ordinary course of business.

cfr-1027.100-release_holdout-01.text: 31 CFR § 1027.100 defines "covered goods" for dealers in jewels, precious metals, and precious stones, including finished goods, and requires dealers to apply anti-money laundering program requirements to transactions involving such goods.

cfr-1027.100-release_holdout-02.text:
31 CFR § 1027.100

This section defines "covered goods" for dealers in jewels, precious metals, and precious stones, including finished goods, as jewels, precious metals, or precious stones that a dealer purchases, sells, or otherwise deals in as part of their business, whether in raw or finished form.

cfr-1027.100-release_holdout-03.text: The definition of covered goods for dealers in jewels, precious metals, and precious stones, including finished goods and relevant limits, is governed by 31 CFR § 1027.100.

cfr-1027.100-release_holdout-04.text: The governing provision defines covered goods for dealers in jewels, precious metals, and precious stones, including finished goods, in 31 CFR § 1027.100.

cfr-1028.210-release_holdout-01.text:
31 CFR § 1028.210

This provision requires credit-card-system operators to implement an anti-money laundering (AML) program that includes approval by senior management and independent testing for compliance.

cfr-1028.210-release_holdout-02.text:
31 CFR § 1028.210

Credit-card-system operators must implement an anti-money laundering (AML) program that is approved by their board of directors or senior management and includes independent testing for compliance, as required by 31 CFR § 1028.210.

cfr-1028.210-release_holdout-03.text: Credit-card-system operators must implement and maintain an anti-money laundering (AML) program that is approved by their board of directors or an equivalent governing body, and the program must be independently audited to test its effectiveness. These requirements are governed by 31 CFR § 1028.210.

cfr-1028.210-release_holdout-04.text: The governing provision requires credit-card-system operators to implement an AML program that is approved by their board of directors or an equivalent governing body and to provide for independent testing for compliance. Citation: 31 CFR § 1028.210.

cfr-1029.210-release_holdout-00.text:
31 CFR § 1029.210

A covered loan or finance company must ensure its AML program applies to the activities of its agents and brokers, requiring appropriate risk-based procedures for oversight and compliance.

cfr-1029.210-release_holdout-02.text:
31 CFR § 1029.210

Covered loan or finance companies must develop and implement an anti-money laundering (AML) program that includes risk-based procedures for conducting due diligence on their agents and brokers, ensuring these parties comply with the institution’s AML policies and procedures.

cfr-1029.210-release_holdout-03.text: A covered loan or finance company must establish and implement an AML program that applies to its agents and brokers, but the program need not duplicate procedures reasonably carried out by those agents or brokers. The governing provision is 31 CFR § 1029.210.

cfr-1010.311-familiar-00.text:
Citation: 31 CFR § 1010.311

Explanation: This section requires financial institutions (other than casinos) to file a Currency Transaction Report (CTR) for each transaction in currency of more than $10,000 by, through, or to the institution during any one business day. Multiple currency transactions shall be treated as a single transaction if the financial institution has knowledge that they are by or on behalf of any one person and result in either cash in or cash out totaling more than $10,000 in one business day.

cfr-1010.311-familiar-01.text:
31 CFR § 1010.311

Financial institutions (other than casinos) must file a report for each transaction in currency of more than $10,000 by, through, or to the institution, unless an exemption applies.

cfr-1010.311-familiar-02.text:
31 CFR § 1010.311

This section requires financial institutions (other than casinos) to file a Currency Transaction Report (CTR) for each transaction in currency of more than $10,000 by, through, or to the institution.

cfr-1010.311-familiar-03.text:
31 CFR § 1010.311

The note should state that financial institutions (other than casinos) are required to file a report with FinCEN for each transaction in currency of more than $10,000 by, through, or to the financial institution.

cfr-1010.313-familiar-00.text:
Citation: 31 CFR § 1010.313

Explanation: This section requires financial institutions (other than casinos) to treat multiple currency transactions conducted by or on behalf of the same person in one business day as a single transaction for Currency Transaction Report (CTR) filing purposes. The aggregation applies to transactions at one or more branches of the same institution, and the total amount must exceed $10,000 in currency.

cfr-1010.313-familiar-01.text:
31 CFR § 1010.313

Summary: This section requires financial institutions (other than casinos) to treat multiple currency transactions conducted by or on behalf of the same person in one business day as a single transaction for Currency Transaction Report (CTR) filing purposes. However, the rule applies only if the institution knows, suspects, or has reason to suspect that the transactions are by or on behalf of the same person.

cfr-1010.313-familiar-02.text:
31 CFR § 1010.313

This section requires financial institutions (other than casinos) to aggregate multiple currency transactions conducted by or on behalf of the same person in a single business day when determining whether a Currency Transaction Report (CTR) must be filed.

cfr-1010.313-familiar-03.text:
31 CFR § 1010.313

The note should state that financial institutions (other than casinos) must aggregate multiple currency transactions conducted by or on behalf of the same person in a single business day to determine if a Currency Transaction Report (CTR) is required.

cfr-1010.314-familiar-00.text:
Citation: 31 CFR § 1010.314

Explanation: This section prohibits structuring transactions with one or more domestic financial institutions for the purpose of evading the reporting requirements of 31 CFR § 1010.311 (currency transaction reports for transactions over $10,000). The prohibition applies regardless of whether the person is aware that structuring is illegal, and it covers both individuals and entities. The rule applies even if the evasion is only attempted, not completed, and regardless of whether the funds are legitimate or illicit.

cfr-1010.314-familiar-01.text:
31 CFR § 1010.314

This section prohibits structuring or attempting to structure transactions with one or more domestic financial institutions for the purpose of evading the reporting requirements of 31 CFR § 1010.311 (currency transaction reports). The prohibition applies regardless of whether the person involved is acting on their own behalf or on behalf of another, and regardless of whether the transaction(s) actually succeed in evading reporting.

cfr-1010.314-familiar-02.text:
31 CFR § 1010.314

This section prohibits structuring transactions with the purpose of evading the currency transaction reporting requirements, making it unlawful to break up transactions to avoid triggering reporting thresholds.

cfr-1010.314-familiar-03.text:
31 CFR § 1010.314

The note should state: "It is prohibited for any person to structure or assist in structuring transactions with one or more domestic financial institutions for the purpose of evading the currency transaction reporting requirements."

cfr-1010.430-familiar-00.text:
Citation: 31 CFR § 1010.430

Explanation: This section requires that records required by the Bank Secrecy Act must be retained for five years and must be accessible or retrievable within a reasonable period. The requirement applies unless a different retention period is specifically prescribed elsewhere in the regulations.

cfr-1010.430-familiar-01.text:
31 CFR § 1010.430

Summary: Financial institutions must retain required BSA records for five years and make them available for inspection or reproduction by the Secretary of the Treasury or authorized agencies upon request. This requirement is subject to exceptions or additional requirements specified elsewhere in the regulations.

cfr-1010.430-familiar-02.text:
31 CFR § 1010.430

This section generally requires that records required by the Bank Secrecy Act be retained for five years and be accessible for inspection or reproduction by the appropriate authorities.

cfr-1010.430-familiar-03.text:
31 CFR § 1010.430

The note should state that BSA records must generally be retained for five years and must be made available for inspection or reproduction upon request by the appropriate authorities.

cfr-1010.520-familiar-00.text:
Citation: 31 CFR § 1010.520

Explanation: This section requires financial institutions to search their records for accounts maintained by named suspects when FinCEN relays a government request. The default search scope is for current accounts and those maintained during the preceding 12 months. Institutions must report matches and provide specified account and transaction information, subject to confidentiality and safe harbor provisions.

cfr-1010.520-familiar-01.text:
31 CFR § 1010.520

Summary: When FinCEN relays a government information request about named suspects, financial institutions must search their records for current accounts and accounts maintained during the preceding 12 months. This obligation is limited to the specific named suspects and does not require searching for transactions outside the defined time frame or for individuals not named in the request.

cfr-1010.520-familiar-02.text:
31 CFR § 1010.520

Qualified explanation: This section governs procedures for financial institutions to search their records for accounts or transactions matching named suspects when FinCEN relays a government request, specifying a default five-year record search scope.

cfr-1010.520-familiar-03.text:
31 CFR § 1010.520

The note should state that, by default, the record-search scope for a government information request relayed by FinCEN about named suspects covers transactions occurring within five years preceding the request.

cfr-1010.540-familiar-00.text:
Citation: 31 CFR § 1010.540

Explanation: This section governs voluntary information sharing among financial institutions under the USA PATRIOT Act Section 314(b). It requires that before sharing information, a financial institution must provide notice to FinCEN and take reasonable steps to verify that the counterparty is also an eligible financial institution intending to use the information for identifying and reporting possible money laundering or terrorist activities.

cfr-1010.540-familiar-01.text:
31 CFR § 1010.540

Summary: This section permits eligible financial institutions to voluntarily share information with one another regarding individuals, entities, organizations, and countries suspected of possible terrorist or money laundering activities. Before sharing, a financial institution must submit a notice to FinCEN using the designated form. Shared information may only be used for identifying and reporting suspicious activity and must be protected by appropriate procedures to ensure confidentiality. The rule does not override any other applicable laws or regulations, and participation is voluntary.

cfr-1010.540-familiar-02.text:
31 CFR § 1010.540

This section governs the procedures for voluntary information sharing among financial institutions regarding individuals, entities, organizations, and countries suspected of possible terrorist or money laundering activities, including requirements for notice to FinCEN and counterparty verification.

cfr-1010.540-familiar-03.text:
31 CFR § 1010.540

The note should state that under 31 CFR § 1010.540, eligible financial institutions may share information regarding individuals, entities, organizations, and countries for the purposes of identifying and reporting activities that may involve terrorist acts or money laundering, provided they give notice to FinCEN and take reasonable steps to verify that counterparties are also eligible financial institutions.

cfr-1020.220-familiar-00.text:
Citation: 31 CFR § 1020.220

Explanation: This section requires banks to implement a written Customer Identification Program (CIP) appropriate for their size and type of business. The CIP must enable the bank to form a reasonable belief that it knows the true identity of each customer. The program must include risk-based procedures for verifying the identity of customers, using information such as name, date of birth, address, and identification number, and must specify when and how verification will occur, including procedures for handling discrepancies and recordkeeping.

cfr-1020.220-familiar-01.text:
31 CFR § 1020.220

This section requires banks to implement a written Customer Identification Program (CIP) that enables them to form a reasonable belief that they know the true identity of each customer. The CIP must include risk-based procedures for verifying the identity of customers to the extent reasonable and practicable, and must be appropriate for the bank’s size, location, and type of business. The rule applies to persons opening an account but excludes certain entities such as federally regulated banks and government agencies.

cfr-1020.220-familiar-02.text:
31 CFR § 1020.220

This section requires banks to implement a written Customer Identification Program (CIP) that enables them to form a reasonable belief that they know the true identity of each customer, as part of their anti-money laundering obligations.

cfr-1020.220-familiar-03.text:
31 CFR § 1020.220

The note should state that banks must implement a written Customer Identification Program (CIP) appropriate for their size and type of business, designed to enable the bank to form a reasonable belief that it knows the true identity of each customer.

cfr-1020.320-familiar-00.text:
Citation: 31 CFR § 1020.320

Explanation: This section requires banks to file a Suspicious Activity Report (SAR) when they detect a known or suspected violation of law or a suspicious transaction involving at least $5,000 in funds or assets (or any amount if a suspect can be identified). The requirement applies if the transaction involves potential money laundering, BSA violations, or criminal activity, and includes both attempted and completed transactions. The rule also requires confidentiality and sets timelines for filing.

cfr-1020.320-familiar-01.text:
31 CFR § 1020.320

Summary: Banks must file a suspicious activity report if they detect a known or suspected violation of law or suspicious transaction involving at least $5,000 in funds or assets, where the bank knows, suspects, or has reason to suspect the transaction involves funds from illegal activity, is designed to evade BSA regulations, has no business or apparent lawful purpose, or involves the use of the bank to facilitate criminal activity. The rule does not require reporting for robberies or burglaries reported to law enforcement, or for lost, missing, counterfeit, or stolen securities reported under other regulations.

cfr-1020.320-familiar-02.text:
31 CFR § 1020.320

This section requires banks to file a Suspicious Activity Report (SAR) when they detect known or suspected violations of law or suspicious transactions involving $5,000 or more, making it the controlling BSA section for bank-specific suspicious-transaction reporting triggers.

cfr-1020.320-familiar-03.text:
31 CFR § 1020.320

The note should state that banks are required to file a suspicious activity report (SAR) when they detect a known or suspected violation of law or a suspicious transaction relevant to a possible violation of law or regulation, as specified in 31 CFR § 1020.320.
